Autoresearch

You already run Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, or Muse. Point one of them at a goal and it will keep improving while you sleep.

This is Karpathy's autoresearch idea: pick a constraint, attach a mechanical metric, and let the agent iterate on its own. The gains compound.

Set the GOAL. The agent runs the LOOP. You wake up to results.

You don't need AGI. You need a goal, a metric, and a loop that never quits.

The core skill, bundled runtime, installation, and verification surface work with all five: Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, and Muse. Hook guardrails ship for Claude Code (native hooks) and pi (extension events).

When the metric stalls, fork-and-flush breaks the plateau, the way Cai et al. (arXiv:2610.07447) do it. At 33% and 66% of the budget, or after 5 iterations with no keep, the loop forks fresh-context branches from the best commit so far, runs each briefly, and keeps the winner. Half the branches pick their own ideas (randomness). The other half each get a distinct experiment from a stateless Advisor that reads the results log (Zhang et al., arXiv:2610.07625). Guided: R sets the split. The orchestrator answers a plateau with FORK before it gives up. Details in guide/autoresearch.md.

sem is a semantic version control tool that runs on top of Git. It parses your code with tree-sitter, extracts every function, class, and method as an entity, and diffs at the entity level instead of by lines. So you see "function blahh was modified" instead of "lines x-y changed."

It works in any Git repo with no setup.

SkillsBench is a benchmark that tests whether AI agents can use Skills to complete professional tasks across many domains. The point is to measure how much a model's ability to solve complex real-world tasks improves when it has specialized Skills available.

To test performance in production-like environments where many Skills are installed at once, we adapted SkillsBench into a large-scale multi-Skill setting. In the original SkillsBench setup, each task comes with only the specialized Skill for that task. In our modified setting, every task is evaluated in a global environment containing all 195 specialized Skills, and all other experimental conditions stay the same. The goal is to see whether an agent can find, select, and orchestrate the right Skills from a large installed pool on its own, and organize them into a workflow that completes complex tasks.

We benchmarked vibeskills v4.1.0 on SkillsBench using DeepSeekV4Flash-VE and OpenHands as the baseline evaluation setup. Compared with the baseline without vibeskills, vibeskills raised the mean verifier reward by 21.12 percentage points, cut token consumption by 29.6%, and reduced tool calls by 33.1%.

Agentic Context Engine (ACE)

ACE is the open-source engine behind Kayba. If you'd rather have the whole loop managed for you, from investigating failures to shipping fixes as PRs, get a demo.

Your agent doesn't learn. Every session it repeats the same mistakes, forgets what worked, and ignores what failed. ACE is an open-source engine that adds a persistent learning loop. It also powers Kayba, a managed service that runs this loop for production agents automatically.

Say your agent claims a seahorse emoji exists. ACE reflects on the error, and on the next attempt the agent answers correctly. No human in the loop.

Grounded Docs MCP Server

Your AI coding assistant quotes docs from memory, which means it quotes the wrong versions. Grounded Docs fixes that. It builds a documentation index that matches the library versions you actually use.

Point it at websites, GitHub repositories, npm, PyPI, or local folders. Then search that index through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a command line, or a web UI. Your assistant answers from the docs you gave it, not from what it remembers.

It's an open-source alternative to Context7, Nia, and Ref.Tools.

I built this to parse 257 languages and grammars through tree-sitter AST analysis and in-process resolvers, with compiler-grade resolution for Python, TypeScript / JavaScript, PHP, C#, Go, C, C++, Java, Kotlin, Swift, Zig, Rust, Ruby, Elixir, Ocaml, Haskell, and others.
